target: AG1’s claim that Election Day as a national holiday would directly remove scheduling barriers and make voting easier for millions.
objection: A federal holiday would not reliably eliminate the main barriers to voting, because many low-wage workers in retail, food service, care work, and similar jobs would still have to work on a federal holiday and would still face wage-loss and scheduling constraints. In other words, changing the calendar alone does not guarantee paid time off or easier voting access for the people most constrained by work.

target: AG1’s assumption that a holiday would materially change who can vote rather than merely shifting the date.
objection: A one-day holiday does not address larger structural obstacles such as registration problems, lack of early or absentee voting, long lines, polling-place accessibility, and procedural confusion. Reforms that directly expand voting options are more effective than simply making Election Day a holiday.

target: AG2’s claim that a holiday only shifts the calendar and does not materially change who can vote.
objection: The objection understates the effect of a holiday, because it also reduces family scheduling barriers by closing schools and ending school-day activities, eases daily logistics like travel and errands, and can create practical voting windows even for hourly workers through holiday scheduling changes and shift swapping.

target: AG2’s argument that private employers’ lack of a legal obligation to give paid holiday leave makes a holiday ineffective.
objection: Even without a legal mandate for paid time off, a holiday still reduces scheduling barriers because the day is no longer a normal weekday: schools and many public services close, childcare and transportation coordination becomes easier, and workplaces often adjust hours or staffing in ways that create more opportunities to vote.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday would “reduce or eliminate” work and school scheduling barriers.
objection: Because federal holiday status does not require private employers to provide paid leave, large numbers of hourly workers in sectors that remain open on holidays would still need to work and would still face the same loss-of-wages and schedule-control problems; therefore, the holiday would not reliably remove the barrier for many eligible voters.

target: AG1’s broader claim that a holiday is a dependable way to increase access based on scheduling alone.
objection: A federal holiday can fail to help the workers least able to absorb wage loss, and may even be regressive: it can benefit voters who already have flexibility or employer-provided time off while leaving low-income workers with the same hard choice between voting and losing pay.

target: AG1’s idea that a federal holiday is preferable to other reforms because it addresses scheduling barriers.
objection: More targeted reforms are more reliable: state laws requiring employers to provide time off to vote directly address the exact wage-and-time constraint, and automatic voter registration removes separate administrative barriers that also suppress turnout.

target: AG1’s claim that making the day non-routine would reduce the work-and-school scheduling barriers enough to boost participation.
objection: Research and prior experience indicate that an Election Day holiday by itself is not an effective turnout strategy compared with reforms that directly expand ballot access, so the causal chain from holiday to higher turnout is not reliable.

target: AG1’s assumption that school closures and the holiday setting make childcare and household coordination easier for low-income voters.
objection: For many low-income families, school closures can make childcare harder and more expensive rather than easier, because holidays do not guarantee affordable childcare coverage; the holiday may simply shift the constraint instead of removing it.

target: AG2’s claim that childcare becomes more limited and expensive on holidays, so a national holiday would not help constrained families.
objection: A national holiday can still improve household-level coordination by aligning Election Day with children being out of school and by changing workplace schedules enough that a caregiver may stay home or arrange coverage, so the childcare constraint is not necessarily worse and may be easier to manage.
